mehmed-ii.name: Mehmed II
mehmed-ii.summary: Ottoman sultan (1432–1481), known as the Conqueror, who captured Constantinople in 1453, ending the Byzantine Empire, and expanded Ottoman rule across Anatolia and the Balkans.

manti-food.name: Manti
manti-food.summary: A dumpling dish of spiced meat wrapped in dough, found across Central Asia, West Asia, the South Caucasus and the Balkans, and especially popular in Turkish cuisine.

kayseri.name: Kayseri
kayseri.summary: A large city in Central Anatolia, Turkey, historically known as Caesarea and the ancient capital of Cappadocia.

mantou.name: Mantou
mantou.summary: A white, soft steamed bread or bun popular in northern China, sometimes called a Chinese steamed bun, with a name folk etymology links to a tale about Zhuge Liang.

maxime-rodinson.name: Maxime Rodinson
maxime-rodinson.summary: French historian and sociologist (1915–2004), a Marxist and leading authority on oriental studies, known for his biography of the prophet Muhammad.

kayqubad-i.name: Kayqubad I
kayqubad-i.summary: Seljuq Sultan of Rum who reigned from 1220 to 1237, remembered for expanding the sultanate and for a golden age of architecture and court culture.

k-lliye.name: Külliye
k-lliye.summary: A complex of buildings centered on a mosque in Turkish architecture, often including a madrasa, clinic, kitchens, bakery and hammam, funded by a charitable foundation.

orhan.name: Orhan
orhan.summary: Second sultan of the Ottoman Empire, reigning from 1323/4 to 1362, who conquered much of northwestern Anatolia from the Byzantines and gained a foothold in Europe.

i-znik.name: İznik
i-znik.summary: A town in Bursa Province, Turkey, built on the site of the ancient city of Nicaea, known today for its historic walls and for the famous İznik tiles and pottery.

orhan-gazi-mosque.name: Orhan Gazi Mosque
orhan-gazi-mosque.summary: A historic mosque in Bursa, Turkey, founded by the Ottoman ruler Orhan in 1339–40, among the oldest surviving Ottoman dynastic monuments.

h-davendigar-mosque.name: Hüdavendigar Mosque
h-davendigar-mosque.summary: Historic mosque in Bursa, Turkey, built between 1365 and 1385 as part of a complex commissioned by Ottoman Sultan Murad I, later renovated after an 1855 earthquake.

murad-i.name: Murad I
murad-i.summary: Ottoman sultan from 1362 until his assassination at the Battle of Kosovo in 1389, who made Adrianople his capital and brought most of the Balkans under Ottoman rule.

bursa.name: Bursa
bursa.summary: A city in northwestern Turkey, historically called Prusa, that served as the Ottoman capital from 1335 until the 1360s.

erefeli-mosque.name: Üç Şerefeli Mosque
erefeli-mosque.summary: A 15th-century Ottoman mosque in Edirne, Turkey, completed in 1447, notable for its wide arcaded courtyard and central dome.

edirne.name: Edirne
edirne.summary: A city in northwestern Turkey near the Greek and Bulgarian borders, historically known as Adrianople, that served as the Ottoman Empire's capital from the 1360s until 1453.

fatih-mosque-istanbul.name: Fatih Mosque
fatih-mosque-istanbul.summary: An Ottoman mosque in Istanbul built between 1463 and 1470 on the site of the Church of the Holy Apostles, named for Sultan Mehmed the Conqueror and rebuilt after a 1766 earthquake.

haji-bektash-veli-complex.name: Haji Bektash Veli Complex
haji-bektash-veli-complex.summary: A 13th-century dervish lodge and later mausoleum in central Anatolia built for the Sufi saint Haji Bektash Veli, which became the spiritual headquarters of the Bektashi Order.

haji-bektash-veli.name: Haji Bektash Veli
haji-bektash-veli.summary: An Islamic scholar, mystic and philosopher from Khorasan who lived and taught in Anatolia around 1209 to 1271, revered by Alevis and seen as the eponym of the Bektashi Sufi order.

bektashism.name: Bektashism
bektashism.summary: A Sufi order of Islam that developed in 13th-century western Anatolia, named after the saint Haji Bektash Veli, and spread widely through the Ottoman Empire.

green-mosque-bursa.name: Green Mosque, Bursa
green-mosque-bursa.summary: Part of a larger complex in Bursa, Turkey, the former Ottoman capital before Constantinople's capture in 1453; also called the Mosque of Mehmed I, its name comes from green and blue interior tile decoration.

mehmed-i.name: Mehmed I
mehmed-i.summary: Ottoman sultan (r. 1413–1421) who reunified the empire after a civil war among Bayezid I's sons and restored central Ottoman authority.

cuerda-seca.name: Cuerda seca
cuerda-seca.summary: A technique, Spanish for 'dry cord,' for applying coloured glazes to ceramic tile surfaces.

bayezid-ii.name: Bayezid II
bayezid-ii.summary: Ottoman sultan from 1481 to 1512 who consolidated the empire and resettled Sephardi Jews expelled from Spain throughout Ottoman lands.

koza-han.name: Koza Han
koza-han.summary: Historic caravanserai in the heart of Bursa's historic market district in Turkey.

amasya.name: Amasya
amasya.summary: A city in northern Turkey's Black Sea region, set in a mountain valley along the Yeşilırmak River, with a 7,500-year history as a provincial capital, known for Ottoman-era wooden houses and rock-cut royal tombs.

bimaristan.name: Bimaristan
bimaristan.summary: A hospital in the historic Islamic world, also known as dar al-shifa ('house of healing') in Arabic or darüşşifa in Turkish.

firuz-agha-mosque.name: Firuz Ağa Mosque
firuz-agha-mosque.summary: A 15th-century Ottoman mosque in Istanbul built by Firuz Ağa, treasurer to Sultan Beyazıt II, near other historic landmarks in the city's old center.

hippodrome-of-constantinople.name: Hippodrome of Constantinople
hippodrome-of-constantinople.summary: The sporting and social centre of Constantinople, a circus for horse and chariot racing in the Eastern Roman Empire; today it survives as Istanbul's Sultanahmet Square.

seljuk-empire.name: Seljuk Empire
seljuk-empire.summary: A medieval Turco-Persian empire founded in 1037 by brothers Tughril and Chaghri, stretching from Anatolia to Central Asia, whose 1071 victory at Manzikert weakened Byzantine control there.

oghuz-turks.name: Oghuz Turks
oghuz-turks.summary: A western Turkic people whose 8th-century tribal confederation in Central Asia became the ancestors of today's Turkmen, Azerbaijanis and Turks.

battle-of-manzikert.name: Battle of Manzikert
battle-of-manzikert.summary: 1071 battle in which the Seljuk Turks decisively defeated the Byzantine Empire and captured Emperor Romanos IV, opening the way for Turkish settlement of Anatolia.

romanos-iv-diogenes.name: Romanos IV Diogenes
romanos-iv-diogenes.summary: Byzantine emperor from 1068 to 1071, remembered chiefly for his defeat and capture at the Battle of Manzikert in 1071, a blow that weakened Byzantine control of Anatolia.

malazgirt.name: Manzikert (Malazgirt)
malazgirt.summary: Town in eastern Turkey, historically called Manzikert, site of the 1071 battle where Seljuk Turks decisively defeated the Byzantines and captured their emperor.

turkification.name: Turkification
turkification.summary: A process by which populations or places take on Turkic culture, language or identity, often used specifically for Ottoman or Turkish Republic policies toward ethnic minorities.

battle-of-k-se-da.name: Battle of Köse Dağ
battle-of-k-se-da.summary: 1243 battle in which a Mongol army decisively defeated the Sultanate of Rum, reducing it to a Mongol client state and paving the way for Mongol control of Anatolia.

sultanate-of-rum.name: Sultanate of Rum
sultanate-of-rum.summary: Turco-Persian Muslim state the Seljuk Turks established over conquered Byzantine Anatolia after 1071, considered the beginning of Turkish history in the region.

ilkhanate.name: Ilkhanate
ilkhanate.summary: A Mongol khanate established by Hülegü, grandson of Genghis Khan, ruling Iran and neighboring lands from 1259; it converted to Islam under Ghazan and collapsed after ruler Abu Sa'id died in 1335.

mesud-ii.name: Mesud II
mesud-ii.summary: Sultan of Rûm between 1284 and 1308, though only as a powerless vassal of the Mongols under Mahmud Ghazan; he died in 1308 as the last of the Seljuks of Rum.

timur.name: Timur (Tamerlane)
timur.summary: Turco-Mongol conqueror (1320s–1405) who founded the Timurid Empire across Central Asia and the Middle East, seen as one of history's greatest and most brutal military leaders.

bayezid-i.name: Bayezid I
bayezid-i.summary: Ottoman sultan from 1389 to 1402 nicknamed 'the Thunderbolt', who conquered Anatolia but was defeated and captured by Timur in 1402, dying in captivity.

ubuk.name: Çubuk
ubuk.summary: A district and municipality of Ankara Province in Turkey, on a flat plain about 35 km north of the city of Ankara.

constantine-ix-monomachos.name: Constantine IX
constantine-ix-monomachos.summary: Byzantine emperor from 1042 to 1055 who gained the throne through marriage to Empress Zoë, sharing rule with her sister Theodora during one of the era's most consequential reigns.

alp-arslan.name: Alp Arslan
alp-arslan.summary: Second sultan of the Seljuk Empire, who reigned from 1063 until his assassination in 1072 and greatly expanded Seljuk territory.

john-skylitzes.name: John Skylitzes
john-skylitzes.summary: Byzantine historian of the late 11th century (early 1040s–after 1101).

iberia-theme.name: Iberia (theme)
iberia-theme.summary: A Byzantine administrative and military province carved from Georgian and Armenian lands in the 11th century, ending with Seljuk invasions in 1074.

ani.name: Ani
ani.summary: A ruined medieval city, now in Turkey, that was capital of the Armenian Bagratuni kingdom from 961 to 1045, growing to perhaps 100,000 people before being sacked by the Mongols in 1236 and later abandoned.

baiju-noyan.name: Baiju Noyan
baiju-noyan.summary: A Mongol commander active in Persia, Armenia, Anatolia and Georgia who succeeded Chormagan and was the last direct imperial governor of the Mongol Near East, dying around 1258.

kaykhusraw-ii.name: Kaykhusraw II
kaykhusraw-ii.summary: Sultan of the Seljuqs of Rum from 1237 to 1246, defeated by the Mongols at the Battle of Köse Dağ in 1243 and died as their vassal.

erzurum.name: Erzurum
erzurum.summary: A city in eastern Turkey over 1,900 meters above sea level, built on the site of the ancient city of Theodosiopolis.

konya.name: Konya (Iconium)
konya.summary: City in central Turkey known in antiquity as Iconium, later capital of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum, and today the spiritual centre of the Whirling Dervishes.

roussel-de-bailleul.name: Roussel de Bailleul
roussel-de-bailleul.summary: A Norman adventurer who served as a soldier under Byzantine emperor Romanos IV Diogenes, ruled 1068–71.

amorium.name: Amorium
amorium.summary: A city in Phrygia, Asia Minor, founded in the Hellenistic period, that flourished under the Byzantine Empire and declined after an Arab sack in 838.

suleiman-ibn-qutalmish.name: Suleiman ibn Qutalmish
suleiman-ibn-qutalmish.summary: Seljuk Turkish leader who founded an independent state in Anatolia and ruled as Sultan of Rûm from 1077 until his death in 1086.

osman-i.name: Osman I
osman-i.summary: Eponymous founder of the Ottoman Empire, who died in 1323 or 1324; almost nothing factual survives about him since no written sources date from his lifetime.

stefan-lazarevi.name: Stefan Lazarević
stefan-lazarevi.summary: Serbian prince from 1389 and later despot from 1402 until 1427, regarded as one of the finest knights of his time, who ruled first as an Ottoman vassal and then as a Hungarian ally.

nicaea.name: Nicaea
nicaea.summary: An ancient Greek city in northwestern Anatolia, site of the first and seventh Ecumenical Councils and source of the Nicene Creed, later capital of the Empire of Nicaea and briefly of the Ottomans.

battle-of-pelekanon.name: Battle of Pelekanon
battle-of-pelekanon.summary: A June 1329 battle in which an Ottoman army under Orhan I defeated a Byzantine relief force led by Andronikos III, sealing the fate of besieged Nicaea, which surrendered two years later.

yunus-emre.name: Yunus Emre
yunus-emre.summary: Turkish folk poet and Sufi (1238–1320) who greatly influenced Turkish culture; UNESCO marked 1991 as International Yunus Emre Year.

sufism.name: Sufism
sufism.summary: An Islamic spiritual and ethical discipline concerned with purifying the self, closeness to God, and mystical experience, often described as Islamic mysticism.

diwan-poetry.name: Diwan (poetry)
diwan-poetry.summary: Tradition of poetry collections by a single author across Islamic cultures of West and Central Asia, North Africa and South Asia, dominated by lyric forms such as ghazals.

book-of-dede-korkut.name: Book of Dede Korkut
book-of-dede-korkut.summary: The most famous of the epic dastans of the Oghuz Turks, carrying the values of nomadic Turkic pre-Islamic life and surviving today in only a few manuscripts.

s-leyman-elebi.name: Süleyman Çelebi
s-leyman-elebi.summary: An Ottoman prince and co-ruler of the empire during the Ottoman Interregnum, active from around 1389/90 until his death in 1411.

kaygusuz-abdal.name: Kaygusuz Abdal
kaygusuz-abdal.summary: A 14th-century Turkish folk poet and dervish who completed his Islamic pilgrimage and traveled widely across Western Asia and the Balkans.

song-of-roland.name: Song of Roland
song-of-roland.summary: An 11th-century French epic poem about the Frankish leader Roland's death at the Battle of Roncevaux Pass in 778, and the oldest surviving major work of French literature.

baligant.name: Baligant
baligant.summary: A fictional Emir of Babylon (Cairo) in the medieval epic The Song of Roland, who leads an army to aid King Marsile against Charlemagne and is killed in single combat with him.

charlemagne.name: Charlemagne
charlemagne.summary: King of the Franks from 768 and emperor of the Carolingian Empire from 800, who united most of Western and Central Europe and was the first recognised western emperor since Rome's fall.

anatolian-beyliks.name: Anatolian beyliks
anatolian-beyliks.summary: Turkish principalities in Anatolia ruled by beys, first founded in the late 11th century; one of them, the Ottomans, absorbed the rest to form the Ottoman Empire by the late 15th century.

karamanids.name: Karamanids
karamanids.summary: A Turkish Anatolian principality descended from Oghuz Turks, centred on the Karaman region, that became one of Anatolia's most powerful beyliks from the mid-14th century until 1487.

germiyanids.name: Germiyanids
germiyanids.summary: A Turkish dynasty that controlled parts of western Anatolia from about 1300 to 1429, one of several beyliks that arose after the Mongol invasion.

s-t.name: Söğüt
s-t.summary: A town in Bilecik Province, Turkey, notable as the founding location and first capital of the Ottoman Empire from 1281 to 1335.

mkhitar-gosh.name: Mkhitar Gosh
mkhitar-gosh.summary: Armenian scholar, priest and writer (1130-1213), a leading figure of the Armenian Renaissance.

the-lawcode-datastanagirk-of-mkhitar-gos.name: Datastanagirk'
the-lawcode-datastanagirk-of-mkhitar-gos.summary: A collection of medieval Armenian feudal laws compiled by Mkhitar Gosh in the late 12th century, later given force of law in Cilicia, Poland's Armenian colonies and Georgia.

armenian-kingdom-of-cilicia.name: Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia
armenian-kingdom-of-cilicia.summary: Armenian state formed in the Middle Ages by refugees fleeing the Seljuk invasion of Armenia, centered in Cilicia and a strong ally of the Crusaders; it became a kingdom in 1198.

zakarid-armenia.name: Zakarid Armenia
zakarid-armenia.summary: A medieval Armenian princedom centered on the city of Ani, ruled by the Zakarid-Mkhargrzeli dynasty as vassals of the Kingdom of Georgia, later a Mongol vassal after 1236.

gedei-khan.name: Ögedei Khan
gedei-khan.summary: Second khan of the Mongol Empire (c. 1186–1241) and third son of Genghis Khan, who continued the empire's expansion after his father's death.

darughachi.name: Darughachi
darughachi.summary: An official title in the Mongol Empire for a governor responsible for taxes and administration over a territorial subdivision called a darugha.

candar-dynasty.name: Candar dynasty
candar-dynasty.summary: A Turkic princely dynasty that ruled parts of northern Anatolia from 1291 to 1461, until its territory was absorbed into the Ottoman Empire by Mehmed II.

sinop-turkey.name: Sinop
sinop-turkey.summary: A city on Turkey's Black Sea coast in the ancient region of Paphlagonia, with a 2022 population of about 57,404.

ibrahim-inal.name: Ibrahim Inal
ibrahim-inal.summary: A Seljuk warlord, governor and prince who died in 1060, half-brother of Sultan Tughril, who governed Mosul and Gence and led campaigns extending Seljuk power into Persia and against Byzantium.

kingdom-of-iberia.name: Kingdom of Iberia
kingdom-of-iberia.summary: The Greco-Roman name for the Georgian kingdom of Kartli, centered on eastern Georgia, which adopted Christianity in the 4th century before falling under Persian and later Byzantine influence.

battle-of-kapetron.name: Battle of Kapetron
battle-of-kapetron.summary: 1048 battle near modern Hasankale, Turkey, in which a combined Byzantine-Georgian army repelled an invading Seljuk force in a fierce night engagement.

ibn-al-athir.name: Ibn al-Athir
ibn-al-athir.summary: A Hadith expert, historian and biographer of Arab descent (1160–1233) who settled in Mosul at age 21 to devote himself to the study of history and Islamic tradition.

kaykaus-i.name: Kaykaus I
kaykaus-i.summary: Seljuk Sultan of Rum from 1211 until his death in 1220, and the eldest son of Kaykhusraw I.

empire-of-trebizond.name: Empire of Trebizond
empire-of-trebizond.summary: One of three Byzantine successor states formed after the Fourth Crusade, existing from 1204 in the Pontus region of northeastern Anatolia with Georgian backing.

kaykhusraw-i.name: Kaykhusraw I
kaykhusraw-i.summary: Seljuk Sultan of Rum who ruled 1192 to 1196 and again 1205 to 1211, the youngest son of Kilij Arslan II.

hethum-i.name: Hethum I
hethum-i.summary: Ruler of the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia from 1226 to 1270 who accepted Mongol overlordship, travelled to the Mongol court at Karakorum, and allied with the Mongols against the Mamluks.

sempad-the-constable.name: Sempad the Constable
sempad-the-constable.summary: A 13th-century noble of Cilician Armenia and older brother of King Hetoum I, serving as diplomat, judge and military commander, and a trusted negotiator with the Mongol Empire.

karakorum.name: Karakorum
karakorum.summary: Capital of the Mongol Empire from 1235 to 1260 and later of the Northern Yuan dynasty, founded in 1220 in what is now Mongolia.

g-y-k-khan.name: Güyük Khan
g-y-k-khan.summary: Third Khagan of the Mongol Empire (reigned 1246–1248), eldest son of Ögedei Khan and grandson of Genghis Khan, who ordered an empire-wide census and held authority over Russian principalities.

alanya.name: Alanya
alanya.summary: Coastal city in Turkey, renamed Ala'iyya (from its earlier name Kalon Oros) in honor of Seljuk sultan Alaeddin Kayqubad I, who left landmarks such as the Red Tower and Alanya Castle.

mersin-province.name: İçel
mersin-province.summary: A province on Turkey's Mediterranean coast between Antalya and Adana, formerly known as İçel Province, with its capital and largest city at Mersin.

k-t-r-m-bayezid.name: Kötürüm Bayezid
k-t-r-m-bayezid.summary: Bey of the Anatolian beylik of Candar from 1361 to 1383.

kastamonu.name: Kastamonu
kastamonu.summary: A city in northern Turkey, seat of Kastamonu Province, with a population of over 125,000.

khorasan.name: Khorasan
khorasan.summary: A historical region of the Iranian Plateau spanning parts of modern Afghanistan, Iran and Central Asia, with boundaries that varied over time and roots reaching back to Bronze Age complex societies there.

alevism.name: Alevism
alevism.summary: A syncretic, mystic movement mainly in Turkey, linked to a Sufi form of Twelver Shi'ism with Central Asian shamanic elements, historically tied to the Bektashi order founded by Haji Bektash Veli.

rumi.name: Rumi
rumi.summary: Sufi mystic and poet (1207–1273) who founded the Mevlevi Order; his Masnavi is considered one of the greatest works of Persian literature.

masnavi.name: Masnavi
masnavi.summary: A six-book Persian poem of about 25,000 verses by Rumi, sometimes called a 'Quran in Persian' and viewed as one of the greatest works of Sufi mystical literature.

old-anatolian-turkish.name: Old Anatolian Turkish
old-anatolian-turkish.summary: The form of Turkish spoken in Anatolia from the 11th to 15th centuries, written in Perso-Arabic script, which developed into early Ottoman Turkish.

sheikh-bedreddin.name: Sheikh Bedreddin
sheikh-bedreddin.summary: An Ottoman mystic, scholar and theologian (1359–1420) best known for leading disciples in a 1416 revolt that challenged Sultan Mehmet I and the Ottoman state.

ardabil.name: Ardabil
ardabil.summary: A city in northwestern Iran and capital of Ardabil province, long known for silk and carpet trade, once briefly the principal city of Azerbaijan, and home to the tomb of Safavid founder Ismail I.

safavid-order.name: Safavid order
safavid-order.summary: A Sufi order founded in Ardabil, renamed the Safaviyya and led by Safi-ad-Din Ardabili from 1301 to 1334; its later leaders sought political power and founded the Safavid dynasty in 1501.

wahdat-al-wuj-d.name: Wahdat al-Wujud
wahdat-al-wuj-d.summary: An Islamic mystical doctrine holding that God is identical with existence itself, attributed to the Sufi Ibn Arabi (d. 1240) and later popular among Sufis despite being condemned by some scholars as heretical.

ganja-azerbaijan.name: Ganja
ganja-azerbaijan.summary: Azerbaijan's third-largest city, historically also known by the Armenian name Gandzak, and capital of the Ganja Khanate until Russia annexed it in 1813.

armenian-renaissance.name: Armenian Renaissance
armenian-renaissance.summary: Period of revival in the Armenian language and literature, roughly from the Crusades to the present, paralleling the European Renaissance.

gregory-of-tatev.name: Gregory of Tatev
gregory-of-tatev.summary: An Armenian philosopher, theologian and saint (1346 to 1409 or 1410) who opposed uniting the Armenian Church with Rome and wrote extensively against Islam, Judaism and other heresies, including in his 1397 Book of Questions, which defended the Armenian Church against Islam and Catholic unionists.

tatev-monastery.name: Tatev Monastery
tatev-monastery.summary: A 9th-century Armenian Apostolic monastery on a basalt plateau in southeastern Armenia, long the bishopric seat of Syunik and a center of regional culture, later hosting a renowned medieval university.

armenian-apostolic-church.name: Armenian Apostolic Church
armenian-apostolic-church.summary: Autocephalous national church of Armenia and one of the oldest Christian churches, tracing its origins to the apostles Bartholomew and Thaddeus and to St. Gregory the Illuminator, its first primate.

shams-tabrizi.name: Shams Tabrizi
shams-tabrizi.summary: An Iranian dervish and poet (1185-1248) best known as the companion who transformed the poet Rumi's life during a period of teaching in Konya.

divan-i-shams-i-tabrizi.name: Divan-i Shams-i Tabrizi
divan-i-shams-i-tabrizi.summary: Collection of over 40,000 verses of Persian lyric poetry by Rumi, written after the disappearance of his teacher Shams-i Tabrizi and dedicated to him, exploring love and longing.

dyophysitism.name: Dyophysitism
dyophysitism.summary: The Christian doctrine that Jesus Christ has two distinct natures, divine and human, held by most denominations but rejected by Oriental Orthodox churches, which favor Miaphysitism instead.

tajiks.name: Tajiks
tajiks.summary: A group of Persian-speaking Eastern Iranian peoples native to Central Asia, forming the largest ethnicity in Tajikistan and a major minority in Afghanistan and Uzbekistan.

seljuk-dynasty.name: Seljuk dynasty
seljuk-dynasty.summary: The Oghuz Turkic, Sunni Muslim ruling family, also called the House of Seljuk, that founded the Seljuk Empire along with the Sultanates of Kermân and Rum, targets of the First Crusade.

caravanserai.name: Caravanserai
caravanserai.summary: A roadside or urban inn common across the Islamic world that sheltered travelers, merchants and pack animals along trade routes such as the Silk Road.

rum-name.name: Rum
rum-name.summary: An exonym derived from 'Romans,' used for the pre-Islamic peoples of Anatolia, the Middle East and the Balkans under the Eastern Roman Empire, and later for Rome and Orthodox Christian minorities.

byzantines.name: Rhomaioi (Byzantines)
byzantines.summary: The Greek name Byzantines used for themselves, meaning "Romans"; they kept this Roman identity even after Constantinople fell and they came under Ottoman rule.

ottoman-claim-to-roman-succession.name: kayser-i rûm
ottoman-claim-to-roman-succession.summary: A title meaning "Caesar of Rome," used by Ottoman sultans after 1453 to press their claim to be legitimate Roman emperors following the conquest of Constantinople.
